body:
A couple asked us as we left the theater, what we thought. Both my husband & I in unison answered "It wasn't what I expected." That being said it was a very thought provoking, dark but enlightening, educational movie.

The movie shows a journey from the point of view & life of each character. It shows both the bad & the good in all. As Americans, we expect happy endings. This movie leaves you wondering if each character's journey was worth the risk.

The entire movie is subtitled, but not difficult to read or completely necessary. The movie is portrayed well enough that you understand the story.

The film was so captivating from start to finish. You realize that the film is showing the turmoil of each stranger. The utter destruction the characters environment plays toward the decisions made in the fleet of a refugee. I cannot lie that I am not an emotional person, but this film had me struggling in tears multiple times. Very dark. Very intimate. Expect major surprises as this is an absolute thriller.

Every main character had a compelling storyline. Omar Sy needs more big roles, the dude is just as good of a villain as he is a hero. All the actors did an amazing job though. It's very difficult to end a movie like this. I naturally didn't expect much but the ending was literally perfect. This movie is definitely worth your time if your on the fence.

I Was a Stranger isn't the kind of film you simply watch-it's the kind you enter. Within minutes, you forget you're sitting on a couch or in a theater, because the story doesn't feel staged. It feels lived-in. The camera, the pacing, the quiet details in each scene all pull you so close that you stop observing the characters and start sharing the weight they carry.

What impressed me most is the editing and structure. The cuts are sharp, purposeful, and emotionally timed. You'll meet a character in the middle of their struggle-no long introductions, no hand-holding-then, just when you think you've understood them, the film slides into their backstory and reframes everything. It's a powerful rhythm: encounter, empathy, revelation. One moment you're indifferent to a stranger on screen, and ten minutes later you're rooting for them like you've known them for years, feeling their fear and hope in your own chest.

And that's the magic here: the movie doesn't beg for your sympathy. It earns it. It turns "that person" into someone, then into us. The struggles aren't packaged as talking points-they're presented as human reality, with all the contradictions and vulnerability that come with it.

More than anything, I Was a Stranger feels important because it refuses to reduce people to sides. Left or right, whatever labels the world wants to use, this story cuts straight through them. It's not propaganda. It's not a debate. It's a reminder that beneath every headline is a human being trying to survive, belong, and be seen.

By the end, you don't just understand the title-you feel it. And you realize: in one way or another, we've all been a stranger too.

So dark. The cinematography was incredible. Acting was absolutely gripping.

At times it was difficult to watch, but that's the purpose of the film. The antagonist is war and it's inescapable reach. Families being torn apart, even over a dinner argument of the 'right' way to deal with refugees.

Inspiring film that feels otherworldly from the short-minded perspective of someone living in the United States of America. Constant reminder that this is reality for so many families.

It was a raw, absolutely riveting, and eye opening movie viewing experience. All around a 10/10 and highly recommend anyone to watch with the expectation of leaving the theater differently than you came in.
